era_setting.place: Puerto Vallarta, Mexico; the Pacific Ocean off Anacapa Island and Point Mugu, California; Oakland and Seattle maintenance facilities, USA
era_setting.notes: The flight is 31 January 2000. The film reaches back to 1985 for the first maintenance interval and forward to the NTSB report of December 2002. Late-1990s American aviation maintenance: paper work cards, dial indicators, hangar lighting, MD-80s. Nothing from the 2010s or 2020s may appear as present day. The 2000-era cockpit is analogue-and-CRT, not glass.

forbidden_claims: That the mechanic who performed the September 1997 end play check was negligent, careless or at fault. The Board placed the cause upstream of him and no charges were ever filed against anyone (FACTS_LEDGER row AK-901). He measured with the only restraining fixture his employer owned, and that fixture did not meet the manufacturer's specification (AK-405).

That Alaska Airlines was prosecuted, fined or found criminally liable. A federal grand jury investigated and in December 2001 federal prosecutors stated that no charges would be filed (FACTS_LEDGER row AK-901).

That the September 1997 end play check produced a specific measurement. No number exists. In-limits readings were not required to be recorded until AD 2000-15-15 in July 2000, and the mechanic could not recall one (FACTS_LEDGER rows AK-309, AK-402).
That the FAA approved the interval extensions out of favouritism, capture or corruption. The report establishes that approvals were given; it establishes no motive (FACTS_LEDGER rows AK-102, AK-103).
That the flight crew made an error or contributed to the accident. The probable cause names no crew action (FACTS_LEDGER row AK-101).
That any specific scheduled lubrication was skipped or missed. The Board found lubrication was insufficient, not that a particular one was omitted (FACTS_LEDGER row AK-101).

Any occupant or fatality figure taken from a keyword search of NTSB/AAR-02/01. The report discusses other accidents; the phrase 'all 14 people on board were killed' belongs to Continental Express 2574 at Eagle Lake, Texas, 1991 (FACTS_LEDGER trap note 1). Derive the figure from the load sheet at AK-002.

That the end play readings of 0.043, 0.048 or 0.075 inch were measured on this aeroplane. They belong to Hawaiian Airlines and Delta assemblies examined during the investigation (FACTS_LEDGER rows AK-702, AK-704).

That the jackscrew design was defective or that McDonnell Douglas built an unsafe aeroplane. The design was certified to survive the loss of 90 percent of threads and the failure of one entire thread spiral; what was absent was a contingency for total loss (FACTS_LEDGER rows AK-601, AK-602, AK-603).
That anyone knew the threads were failing. Nothing in the record supports foreknowledge by any person.

That the crew could have saved the aeroplane by acting differently. The Board makes no such finding, and the horizontal stabilizer moved to at least 14 degrees leading edge up (FACTS_LEDGER row AK-014).
That this is a story about one airline. Assemblies from at least two other carriers were found worn during the investigation (FACTS_LEDGER rows AK-702, AK-704).

beats.headline: WE DID EXACTLY WHAT WE WERE TOLD

notes: EP79 of the EP77-82 slate. Runtime and word bands follow the owner's 2026-08-23 decision: 29-32 minutes, divided at the measured 160 wpm, never 176. Source is NTSB/AAR-02/01, downloaded and read at 250 pages, with every quoted string located back to its PDF page in the facts ledger. Eighty-eight people died and the two pilots are on the recorder; forbidden_claims exists mostly to stop this film becoming an accusation against a mechanic who was never charged, and to stop two documented traps in the source itself reaching the screen as fact. The controlling idea, never spoken: an inspection is worth exactly what its instrument is worth. Motif: a dial indicator needle, at rest, being read, reading nothing anyone wrote down, at rest again. forbidden_subjects bans the accident itself entirely -- no wreckage, no impact, no inverted aircraft, no salvage -- so the film is carried by the instrument, the hangar, and the paperwork.
